transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because I’m having a hard time getting near scaffolds or roof edges at work. Even when I can see the rails are up and I know it’s supposed to be safe, my head just tells me I’m about to go over. It’s gotten pretty bad.
Do you ever have episodes where you feel an intense fear or discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes?

Yes. It comes on fast. The second I step onto temporary stairs, or even start walking toward an open upper floor, my chest tightens and my hands get sweaty. I can feel my legs starting to lock up, like I might not be able to take another step.
Is your fear limited to situations involving heights?

Yes, it’s really just heights. Scaffolds, roof edges, upper platforms—those are what set it off. Even when I can see the rails are there and I know it should be safe, my mind goes straight to thinking I’m about to go over.
Has your fear of heights been affecting your ability to do your job or daily activities?

Yes. It’s started causing real problems at work. I’ve missed or put off enough upper-level walk-throughs that my crews and some subcontractors are questioning my decisions. And it’s gotten to the point where my employer’s insurer wanted an occupational health review because I wasn’t getting key safety inspections done.
Do you find yourself avoiding situations or places that involve heights because of this fear?

Yes. I avoid them whenever I can. I’ve been handing off inspections at height to my foremen, and I try to move meetings down to ground level if there’s any way to do it. If I absolutely have to go up, I make sure someone is right beside me, and I just rush through it scared the whole time.
Has your fear of heights affected your relationships with family or friends?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed it causing a lot of problems with family or friends, at least not in a clear way. Most of it has been more around work and avoiding those height situations.
Do you think the episodes of intense fear or discomfort you experience in height situations qualify as panic attacks?

I don’t know if I’d call them panic attacks exactly, but it feels pretty close. The second I step onto temporary stairs or even start walking toward an open upper floor, my chest tightens, my hands get sweaty, and my legs feel like they might lock up before I can take another step.
How long have you been experiencing this fear of heights?
It’s been about thirteen months now, since that stair tower accident. Before that, I didn’t really have this kind of fear.
Is your fear more about the height itself or about falling from that height?

It’s more about falling, I think. Like if I’m near a scaffold, a roof edge, or an upper platform, my head just tells me I’m going to go over—even when I can see the rails are there and I know it’s supposed to be safe.
Is your fear of heights ever triggered by simply looking at a height from a safe distance, without being at risk of falling?

Not usually just looking from far away. It’s when I have to get near it—like a scaffold, a roof edge, or an upper platform. Even if I can see the rails are there and it should be safe, my head still tells me I’m about to go over.
Has your fear of heights started to affect your social life or relationships with friends and family in any way?

I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed it causing big problems with friends or family, at least not directly. I mean, it affects work situations more than anything, but socially… I don’t think it’s changed much.
Has your fear of heights caused you to avoid social gatherings or events that involve heights, such as outings to high places or events at venues with high balconies or rooftops?

It’s more at work than social events, honestly. I’ve been handing off height inspections to my foremen, or moving meetings down to ground level if I can. If I absolutely have to go up, I keep someone right next to me and just rush through it, scared the whole time.
